PAPER: Artificial Intelligence Review (2026) 59:20 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11371-y Neural network-based prediction of SMTP errors and bounces in cold emailing: a comparative study of GRU, CNN, and TCN Anna Jach1 Received: 9 April 2025 / Accepted: 26 August 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract The cold email industry faces significant challenges in ensuring successful message de- livery, with SMTP errors and bounces being common occurrences. Predicting these errors can help optimize email delivery and improve senders’ reputation. In this study, the abili- ties of Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and Tem- poral Convolutional Network (TCN) were examined to predict SMTP errors and bounces in the context of a cold email dataset. The study reveals that both the GRU networks and the CNNs have achieved over 70% accuracy in predicting SMTP errors and bounces. Exploiting all three architectures, GRU, MLP, and TCN, can substantially enhance the management and optimization of the cold email sending process, leading to improved email delivery rates and better sender reputation. Keywords Cold email · SMTP errors · Email deliverability · Predictive analysis 1 Introduction Cold emailing is a marketing strategy in which businesses or individuals send emails to potential customers (prospects). The purpose is to introduce a product, service, or opportu- nity with the aim of initiating a conversation, generating leads, or making sales. Cold email- ing differs from spam in that it is typically sent to people who might have some relevance to the sender’s offering. Efficient cold email delivery is crucial for businesses and market- ers. However, SMTP errors and bounces can diminish deliverability and negatively impact senders’ reputation. Predicting these errors or anomalies in advance can help implement corrective measures and enhance overall email performance. Anomalies in the cold email industry might include sudden spikes in sending volume, unusual patterns in email open rates, or unexpected changes in response rates. Although the prediction of SMTP errors and bounces in cold emailing remains relatively unexplored, it conceptually overlaps with established domains such as time-series forecast- ing and anomaly detection. The temporal and sequential nature of email sending patterns and error occurrences aligns with challenges commonly addressed in these domains. While direct comparisons with existing models are limited due to the unique dataset and problem specifics, this work contributes to bridging the gap between domain-specific email deliver- ability issues and general time-dependent anomaly prediction techniques. This study considers one of the major email service providers, the dataset contains data from free email accounts and addresses within a purchased domain as well. 1.1 Research contributions This paper presents a structured comparison of three neural network architectures, GRU, CNN, and TCN, for predicting SMTP errors based on sequential metadata. The main con- tributions are as follows: ● A comparative empirical evaluation of GRU, CNN, and TCN models, demonstrating that despite GRU’s superior training metrics, TCN offers the best generalization perfor- mance, achieving the highest accuracy and F1-score on unseen data, ● Identification and analysis of overfitting patterns in GRU, reinforcing the importance of evaluating generalization, ● Integration of classical machine learning methods (SVM and Random Forest) as base- line references, highlighting the relative advantage of sequence-based deep learning approaches, ● A scalable preprocessing and evaluation pipeline suitable for similar anomaly detection tasks using limited temporal metadata. Collectively, these contributions aim to support the development of more reliable cold email systems and demonstrate the value of applying sequential modeling techniques to real-world deliverability challenges. 2 Related works The problem of ensuring high email deliverability in the cold email industry has been explored through various approaches, with recent advances in machine learning and neural networks offering promising solutions. Three neural network architectures have been examined: Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN). GRU networks work as an alternative to Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, which incorporate gated recurrent units. These units enable the neural network to capture long-term dependencies in sequential data while mitigating issues such as vanishing gradi- ents, making them particularly suitable for time series prediction tasks. CNN networks use layers with convolutional filters to automatically learn spatial hier- archies of features, making them highly effective at tasks such as image recognition and classification. CNNs consist of multiple layers, including convolutional, pooling, and fully connected layers, which work together to capture and abstract patterns from raw input data, allowing the network to learn complex representations. Additionally, features such as email con- tent or metadata may have been incorporated, depending on their relevance to the prediction task. The preprocessing steps involved several stages. First, the message sending time was converted into numerical values and normalized to a range between 0 and 1. The target labels were binarized - all instances indicating an error were assigned the value 1, while the rest were labeled 0. Four key features (as mentioned in Table 1) were selected as model inputs. Missing values were handled by replacing them with zeros. Finally, the data was reshaped into a format required by sequential models such as recurrent and convolutional neural networks. 5.2 Data splitting The dataset, consisting of 50,343 entries, was divided into training, validation, and test- ing sets to facilitate model training, hyperparameter tuning, and performance evaluation. To address the imbalance between the two considered classes (errors and non-errors), the SMOTE technique was applied to balance the dataset. Following this, 80% of the data were allocated to the training set for optimizing model parameters, while the remaining 20% were split between the testing and validation sets. The validation set was used to select the best- performing model through hyperparameter tuning, and the testing set was reserved for the final performance assessment, ensuring an unbiased evaluation of the models. 5.3 Model training and evaluation Each neural network architecture explored in this study (GRU, CNN, TCN) was trained using the training dataset, with hyperparameters tuned to optimize the predictive capabili- ties. The parameters of the neural network architectures used, as well as the learning rates, were determined experimentally. Multiple configurations were tested to identify the optimal 1 3 20 Page 14 of 21 A. Jach settings for the specific characteristics of the dataset and the problem domain. This approach allows for the selection of the most effective models. The first neural network architecture used in this study is a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) model. The model was built using Keras’ Sequential API and achieved an accuracy of 80.97% over 137 epochs. The architecture consists of three GRU layers, three dropout layers and an output layer with a single unit. First GRU layer: The first layer is a GRU with 15 units and return_sequences=True, meaning that it outputs the entire sequence instead of just the last time step. This is crucial for retaining the temporal structure of the input data across multiple GRU layers. Dropout layer: A dropout layer with a rate of 20% is applied after the first GRU to pre- vent overfitting by randomly setting 20% of the neurons to zero during training. Dropout layer: A second dropout layer with a rate of 10% follows the second GRU layer to reduce overfitting. Second GRU layer: The second GRU layer contains 50 units and uses return_ sequences=True, allowing the network to further capture temporal dependencies across a longer sequence of data. Third GRU layer: This layer contains 15 units but without return_sequences, meaning that only the final output of the sequence is passed to the next layer. This helps condense the sequence data for the final prediction. Dropout layer: Another dropout layer with a rate of 20% is applied after the third GRU layer to improve generalization. Dense output layer: The final output layer is a Dense layer with a single unit, which predicts the likelihood of occurring an SMTP error or bounce. The network is compiled using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.0001. The loss function is set to the mean squared error (MSE), and accuracy is used as the evaluation metric. To prevent overfitting and ensure a robust model, early stopping was implemented using the EarlyStopping callback, monitoring the loss and stopping the training process after 30 epochs if no further improvement was observed. The model was trained on 80% of the data, with 20% allocated for validation, using a batch size of 512 and for a maximum of 2000 epochs. However, due to early stopping, train- ing was halted at 137 epochs. In terms of model complexity, the network contains a total of 13,891 parameters (approximately 54.26 KB). All the parameters are trainable, which means that they are optimized during the training process to improve model performance. The model evaluation achieved an accuracy of 82.03%, demonstrating strong performance in predicting SMTP errors and bounces. The model was compiled using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.000001. The Adam optimizer is known for its adaptive learning rate, which helps achieve faster convergence. A very small learning rate was chosen to ensure stable and gradual updates to the model parameters. The model uses the mean squared error (MSE) as the loss func- tion, which is appropriate for regression tasks and allows the network to minimize the error between the predicted and actual bounce/error values. To prevent overfitting and unnecessary training, early stopping was implemented. The training process monitored the loss and automatically stopped after 50 epochs if no further improvement was observed. The model was trained with 500 epochs and a batch size of 512, with 85% of the data for training and 15% for validation. The total number of parameters in the model is 20 451 (approximately 79.89 KB), with all the parameters being trainable. The third neural network architecture implemented in this study is based on Tempo- ral Convolutional Networks (TCN), combined with convolutional layers and dropout. The model is structured as follows: Input layer: The input shape reflects the time-step and feature dimensions of the dataset, which has been split into training and validation sets (85% for training, 15% for validation). First TCN layer: The first layer is a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with 32 filters, a kernel size of 3, and tanh activation. TCNs are particularly suited for sequential data tasks, as they effectively capture both short-term and long-term dependencies through causal convolutions, which ensures that predictions at any point depend only on past and present data. Batch normalization layer: Following the first TCN layer, Batch Normalization is applied to stabilize and accelerate training by normalizing the output from the previous layer. Dropout layer: A dropout rate of 40% is introduced to prevent overfitting by randomly deactivating 40% of the neurons during each training step, which helps the network general- ize better on unseen data. 1 3 20 Page 16 of 21 A. Jach Conv1D layer: Next, a Conv1D layer with 16 filters and a kernel size of 3 is added. This layer uses tanh activation and incorporates L2 regularization (with a regularization factor of 0.01) to further prevent overfitting by penalizing large weights. Batch normalization layer: Another Batch normalization layer is applied after the Conv1D layer to normalize its output, making the training process more efficient and reduc- ing the internal covariate shift. Dropout layer: A second dropout layer with a 40% rate is introduced for additional regularization, helping the model become more robust. Second TCN layer: A second TCN layer with 8 filters, a kernel size of 3, and tanh activation is included, with return_sequences=False, meaning that only the final output of the sequence is passed to the next layer. This helps condense the sequential data for binary classification. Dense output layer: The output layer is a Dense layer with 1 unit and sigmoid acti- vation, which is suitable for binary classification tasks, and outputs a probability value between 0 and 1. The model was compiled using the Adadelta optimizer with a reduced learning rate of 0.0001. Adadelta is a robust gradient-based optimizer that dynamically adjusts the learn- ing rate for each parameter, which can be particularly helpful when working with sparse gradients. The model uses binary cross-entropy as the loss function, which is appropriate for binary classification tasks such as predicting whether an email will bounce or not. The training is stopped when no further improvement is detected for 10 epochs, with the best model weights being restored after stopping. The learning rate is dynamically reduced by a factor of 0.5 if the validation loss does not improve after 5 epochs, with a minimum learning rate of 0.00001. After training the model for the specified number of epochs, the model achieved a vali- dation accuracy of 77%, indicating that it performs well in predicting SMTP errors and bounces. Comparative analysis highlights the strengths and weaknesses of the GRU, MLP, and TCN in predicting SMTP errors and bounces. 6 Results The primary objective of this evaluation is to determine whether any of the three neural network architectures can forecast anomalies in the email-sending process with accuracy exceeding 75%, and to identify which achieves the lowest Mean Squared Error (MSE) dur- ing both training and testing phases. The results presented above indicate that the three neural network architectures achieve varying levels of performance in forecasting anomalies in the process of sending messages. The evaluation criteria include accuracy, Mean Squared Error (MSE) during both training and testing, and the F1-score during testing. To better illustrate the differences highlighted in Table 2, Fig. 6 presents a comparative chart of training and testing metrics for each model. The chart visualizes the training and testing results separately, emphasizing differ- ences in accuracy, MSE, and F1-score. Notably, the TCN consistently offers the best balance between test accuracy and F1-score, while avoiding the marked performance drop observed in the GRU. 1 3 Neural network-based prediction of SMTP errors and bounces in cold… Page 17 of 21 20 Table 2 Training and testing GRU CNN TCN accuracy for three examined Training accuracy 82.03% 72% 77% architectures Training MSE 13.63% 16.43% 14.21% Testing MSE 12.53% 19.63% 18.32% Testing accuracy 59% 58% 61% Testing F1-score 60% 67% 65% Fig. 6 Performance metrics comparison for the three neural networks The GRU achieved the highest training accuracy (82.03%) and the lowest MSE during both training and testing. It recorded the highest testing accuracy and a com- petitive F1-score, indicating it generalizes better than the GRU and slightly better than the CNN. The TCN is the most effective model among the three architectures evaluated. This con- clusion is based on its ability to generalize to unseen data, as indicated by the smallest difference between training and testing accuracy, which reflects a lower risk of overfitting compared to the GRU and CNN. The TCN also achieves the highest accuracy on the test set (61%), outperforming both GRU and CNN in correctly classifying new samples. Addition- ally, it maintains a strong balance between precision and recall, demonstrated by a competi- tive testing F1-score of 65%, which is crucial for anomaly detection tasks. While the GRU demonstrates superior performance during training, its significant drop in testing metrics raises concerns about overfitting. The CNN shows the highest MSE and lowest accuracy despite a decent F1-score. Overall, the TCN’s combination of high test accuracy, robust F1-score, and reduced overfitting risk makes it the most reliable and balanced choice for predicting SMTP errors and bounces in this study. These results reinforce the earlier observation: while GRU performs well during training, it suffers from overfitting, and TCN offers a more consistent balance across all metrics, despite its lower AUC (Fig. 8). Two classical baselines were also evaluated for comparison: Support Vector Machine with an RBF kernel, and Random Forest. The SVM achieved an AUC of 0.818 – the highest among all models – and a testing accuracy of 63.2%, but had a very low F1-score (0.041), indicating poor performance in handling class imbalance. Similarly, the Random For- est achieved the highest raw accuracy (77.6%) among all models and a respectable AUC of 0.753, yet also struggled with an F1-score of just 0.040. These findings suggest that although classical models like SVM and Random Forest may achieve high AUC values, their practical utility is limited due to an inability to effectively manage uneven class dis- tributions. Neural models – particularly the TCN – provide a more balanced solution for anomaly detection, maintaining competitive accuracy and superior F1-score while better generalizing to new data. Therefore, the TCN is identified as the most effective architecture in this research. As shown in Table 3, classical models such as SVM and Random Forest achieved high test accuracy (63.2% and 77.6%, respectively) and AUC values, with SVM reaching the highest AUC (0.818). However, their F1-scores remain extremely low (around 4%), indicat- ing poor performance in detecting anomalies and strong class imbalance effects. In contrast, deep learning models, particularly the TCN, demonstrated superior balance across met- rics: achieving the highest test accuracy among neural networks (61%) and a competitive F1-score (65%) with low overfitting risk. Despite lower AUC scores, the TCN model’s consistency in handling both majority and minority classes makes it the most robust choice for anomaly detection in cold emailing workflows. 7 Conclusions and future research Anomaly detection in the cold email industry using GRU and CNN networks presents a complex yet promising approach. Since no direct comparison can be made with the state- of-the-art methods due to the absence of relevant literature for this specific type of data, this work represents a first step toward addressing this gap. Future work will involve developing benchmarks to compare the performance of this neural network-based solution with poten- tial alternative methods as they emerge. Additionally, it is planned to investigate the potential improvements this system could bring to the cold email process if implemented on a larger scale across all application users. In particular, the goal is to evaluate the impact of this system on email deliverability and verify how much this new system could improve the whole sending process and overall campaign effectiveness. Further research will also include the implementation of transformers, which may pro- vide even more robust and efficient anomaly detection capabilities. The next phase will involve deploying the trained models in a production environment and conducting thorough testing, followed by continuous performance monitoring and iterative enhancements based 1 3 20 Page 20 of 21 A. Jach on real-world feedback. Moreover, integrating content-level features (e.g., subject line or message body) may further improve predictive performance in complex scenarios. 7.1 Limitations This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. First, the dataset used is specific to a single cold email platform and includes approxi- mately 50,000 records. While sufficient for the selected models, this dataset size and scope may limit generalization abilities of the findings across other industries or platforms. Second, the input features are restricted to temporal and metadata-based attributes. Con- tent-related information, such as subject lines, email body, or recipient engagement signals was not included. As a result, the models do not account for semantic or behavioral factors that may significantly influence email deliverability. Third, the evaluation was conducted on a static dataset without addressing concept drift or changes in data distribution over time. Real-world applications would require ongoing model updates and monitoring, which are outside the scope of this study. Finally, while modern architectures such as transformers and hybrid attention-based models are acknowl- edged as promising, they were not employed due to dataset size and complexity constraints. Future work will explore these alternatives in more expansive, feature-rich settings. JSON: Name: smtp_error_predict_seq_models Title: Comparative evaluation of GRU, 1D-CNN, and TCN sequence models for predicting SMTP errors and bounces in cold-email metadata streams Short Hypothesis: When trained on sequential cold-email metadata, Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) produce a higher test F1-score for SMTP error and bounce prediction than GRU and 1D-CNN architectures under identical training and class-imbalance handling conditions. Related Work: Prior approaches to email deliverability and anomaly detection span classical classifiers (Random Forest, SVM) operating on aggregated SMTP features, RNN-based sequence models (LSTM/GRU) for temporal traffic forecasting, convolutional and hybrid networks for short-sequence pattern extraction, and unsupervised/time-series representation methods (autoencoders, adversarially trained detectors) for anomaly discovery. Transformer-like architectures have been proposed for long-horizon forecasting but require large datasets and can lose temporal locality without modifications. Existing methods exhibit several limitations for SMTP error prediction: classical models ignore sequence order and temporal context; simple RNNs can overfit on small industrial datasets and suffer vanishing-gradient/long-dependency issues; CNNs with short receptive fields can miss long-range dependencies; unsupervised detectors require carefully tuned thresholds and labeled validation data; and transformer solutions generally need orders of magnitude more training data. Additionally, evaluation in the domain is confounded by severe class imbalance, inconsistent label formats across providers, and a lack of standardized benchmarks. Abstract: This research pipeline addresses prediction of SMTP errors and bounces in cold-email sending workflows using sequence-aware neural models. We propose a controlled comparative evaluation of GRU, one-dimensional CNN, and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) architectures trained on per-message sequential metadata (timestamps, domain age, sender and mailbox identifiers, and error/bounce labels). The main contribution is a rigorous experimental protocol that measures generalization under temporal splitting, class imbalance handling, and model-regularization strategies, and that reports precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, and calibration metrics. We also include classical baselines (SVM, Random Forest, MLP) and targeted ablations to isolate the effects of sequence modeling, receptive field size, and sampling-based balancing. Expected outcomes are: (1) quantification of relative generalization performance across architectures on industrial cold-email metadata; (2) identification of overfitting signatures and sensitivity to class imbalance; and (3) a reproducible evaluation pipeline and benchmark to guide future deliverability models and deployment decisions. Experiments: Datasets: Use the industrial cold-email metadata dataset described in the report (50,343 messages from 13 mailboxes over 60 days; features: send timestamp, domain age in days, user ID, mailbox ID, error/bounce timestamp/label). Produce two additional derived variants: (A) anonymized ID embeddings for user/mailbox; (B) temporally-augmented sequences with fixed-length windows (window sizes: 8, 32, 128 messages per sender). Splits: use time-aware splitting: first 70% of chronological data for training, next 10% for validation, final 20% for testing. Also run K-fold blocked time-series cross-validation (k=5) for robustness. Preprocessing: scale numeric fields to [0,1]; encode IDs via learned embeddings; replace missing values with dedicated indicator values; do not use message content. Class-imbalance handling: compare three strategies: (1) no balancing, (2) SMOTE on training set only, (3) class-weighted loss. Models and baselines: train GRU (stacked, hidden sizes {16,48,16}, dropout {0.1,0.2}), 1D-CNN (filters {30,80,160,30}, kernel sizes {1,3}), TCN (dilations to cover short and long-range dependencies; filter counts {32,16,8}; kernel size 3), MLP (two hidden layers 128/64), SVM-RBF (grid over C,gamma), Random Forest (n_estimators {100,500}). Training: batch size 256, early stopping on validation F1 (patience 10), repeated runs (n=10) with different seeds per configuration. Hyperparameter search: random search 50 trials per model on validation F1. Evaluation metrics: primary metric F1-score (positive class), secondary metrics precision, recall, PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, calibration (Brier score), and mean squared error for probabilistic outputs. Ablations/comparisons: (i) sequence-aware vs non-sequence baselines (MLP/RF/SVM), (ii) receptive-field ablation for TCN and CNN (vary dilation depth and kernel size), (iii) balancing method ablation (SMOTE vs class weights vs none), (iv) training-data-size scaling (use 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of training set) to measure data-efficiency. Statistical testing: report mean±std over 10 runs and perform paired bootstrap significance tests between TCN and nearest competitor on test F1 (alpha=0.05). Reproducibility: record seed, environment, and final model checkpoints; provide code to load anonymized metadata and run the pipeline. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data representativeness: dataset is limited to 13 mailboxes and a single provider, constraining external validity across ESPs, domains, and geographic regions. Label and format variability: SMTP error semantics differ across providers and may introduce noisy or inconsistent labels that degrade supervised learning. Class imbalance and low positive prevalence: rare-error class can yield unstable F1 estimates and optimistic AUCs; synthetic oversampling may produce unrealistic minority examples. Temporal leakage and nonstationarity: naive random splits risk leakage; concept drift over time can invalidate offline evaluation and hamper deployment. Overfitting: deep sequence models (GRU, CNN, TCN) may fit idiosyncratic sender patterns given limited data, producing high train but low test performance. Compute and scalability: hyperparameter searches and repeated runs for statistical confidence require substantial compute; TCN dilation depth increases memory and latency for long windows. Interpretability and operationalization: model decisions based on anonymized IDs and timestamps are weakly explainable for remediation actions. Privacy and contractual constraints: data are proprietary; sharing and independent replication may be restricted. Ethical and compliance limits: models acting on deliverability could affect third-party recipients or sender reputations in ways not captured by offline metrics.
